content.title: About
content.content: Whipped cream is a light, airy dessert topping made by beating high‑fat dairy cream (typically 30‑36 % milk fat). The beating process creates a stable emulsion that holds air bubbles, giving the cream a soft, fluffy texture. It is commonly used to top cakes, pastries, hot drinks, and fresh fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally whipped cream was made by hand, but today most producers use mixers and stabilizers.
Stabilizers such as gelatin, starch, or commercial food stabilizers are often added to improve holding power.
Whipped cream can be flavored with vanilla, chocolate, caramel, or fruit purées.
In the United States, aerosol “spray” whipped cream is popular; nitrogen or nitrous oxide propels the cream and helps it keep its shape.
Cream used for whipping must contain at least 30 % fat; lower‑fat creams do not form a stable foam.

items.title: Source of Vitamin A
items.content: Cream is rich in vitamin A, which supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Contains Vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D in cream aids calcium absorption and promotes bone health.

items.title: Contains Fat‑Soluble Vitamins
items.content: Vitamins E and K present in cream have antioxidant and blood‑clotting benefits.

items.title: Calcium and Phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy Dense
items.content: The fat in cream provides a quick source of energy, useful during high‑intensity activities.

items.title: High Fat and Calorie Content
items.content: Large servings can contribute to weight gain and raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant may experience digestive discomfort after consuming cream.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Saturated Fat
items.content: Excessive intake of saturated fat is linked to increased cardiovascular risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve whipped cream over berries, ice cream, hot chocolate, pancakes, and cakes. It can be folded into mousses, custards, and sauces, or added to coffee and cocktails for a silky, airy finish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep whipped cream refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container and use within 3‑5 days. If the cream is already whipped, store it in an airtight bowl to prevent it from absorbing other odors. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.
